_comment: The redaction check's pattern table -- the GENERIC STARTER, and the one that ships. Read by
Test-PracticeClaims.ps1 check C when redaction-classes.json is not present beside it.
THIS FILE EXISTS BECAUSE THE REAL TABLE CANNOT SHIP. The patterns a redaction gate holds ARE the
strings it forbids, so a populated table is a single-screen list of every internal identifier its
author could think of -- deduplicated, and captioned with why each one matters. That is a useful
artifact inside an organisation and a reconnaissance map outside one, and there is no middle
setting available: a pattern blurred enough to be safe to publish stops matching, and a class
that has stopped matching reports exactly what a clean tree reports. So the populated table is
held back from the distribution, and this one ships in its place.
NOTHING BELOW IS REAL. Every name here is fictional -- example-corp, acme_warehouse,
internal.example.invalid, REC-482913 -- and none of it will match anything in your tree. That is
the shape working as intended, not a defect in it: what ships is the SCHEMA and the reasoning,
and the vocabulary is yours to write.
TO STAND THE GATE UP: copy this file to redaction-classes.json beside it, replace every pattern
with your own organisation's identifiers, and then make sure redaction-classes.json is excluded
from whatever YOU distribute -- it will be a reconnaissance map of your estate for exactly the
same reason. The gate prefers redaction-classes.json and falls back to this file, so until you
write one, every run says in its note that it scanned with placeholder patterns.
NEITHER TABLE IS SCANNED BY THE CHECK IT FEEDS, and both file names sit in the gate's own
self-exemption list for the reason the gate itself does: a class table holds every string it
forbids, so scanning it reports the table rather than the tree. Copy this file to
redaction-classes.json and the exemption comes along with the name. Call it something else and
the gate will not find it at all -- there is no search, only those two names in that order.
AND THAT NOTE IS NOT A FORMALITY. A run against this table forbids example-corp and
acme_warehouse and nothing else. It exercises the plumbing -- the file loads, the classes parse,
every example still matches its own pattern, the scan walks the tree, the report prints -- and it
certifies nothing whatever about your identifiers. Do not read a green Redaction line under these
patterns as evidence of a clean tree; that is the one misreading this file is written to prevent.
REQUIRED KEYS, and what each is for:
name             Appears verbatim in every finding. Write it as the thing being protected, not
as a regex nickname -- the reader of a finding has to know what they hit.
pattern          A .NET regex. CASE-SENSITIVE unless you write (?i): the scan uses
[regex]::Match, and so do the controls, deliberately and for the same reason.
example          A string the pattern MUST match, checked on EVERY run rather than only in a
self-test. A pattern that has stopped matching produces no findings, and no
findings is what a clean tree produces too. This one key is what stands
between a broken class and a gate that silently forbids nothing.
counter_example  Optional, and worth writing wherever the class runs close to legitimate prose:
the near-miss the tree is ALLOWED to carry, asserted NOT to match. A class too
broad fails a clean tree, which teaches people to route around the gate.
reason           Required. What the class protects against. A class without one is somebody's
half-remembered worry, and the next reader cannot tell whether to widen it,
narrow it, or strike it.
THE GATE THROWS RATHER THAN PASSING if neither this file nor redaction-classes.json is present,
or if the table it does load holds no classes. A check that found no patterns has forbidden
nothing, and it must never report PASS.

classes.name: personal path or identity
classes.reason: Named individuals, and the per-account directory convention your scripts assume. Put your own account names and login shapes here. A host path names a person and a machine layout, not just a file, and it is the identifier authors paste most often without noticing. The counter-example is the placeholder form documentation is supposed to use instead: if the class fires on that, it is too broad to live with.

classes.name: organisation
classes.example: ask in the Widget Guild channel
classes.counter_example: a widget factory and a guild of stonemasons
classes.reason: Your employer's name, its mail domain, its internal abbreviations, and its internal community or channel names. The community names are the ones that get missed: they read as warmth rather than as identifiers, yet they tell a recipient which organisation a bundle came from and point them at a forum they cannot join. Write those in explicitly -- a class that matches only the full legal name will pass a document that names three internal channels.

classes.name: organisation written out
classes.reason: Your organisation's name written out with spaces, as a separate class from the closed-up and abbreviated forms. Write BOTH: a class matching only 'examplecorp' or an internal abbreviation will pass a LICENSE or NOTICE naming 'Example Corporation' in full, which is the one place a legal attribution line is guaranteed to spell it out. That gap was real and measured in the tree this table came from.

classes.name: infrastructure
classes.reason: Hostnames, catalog/schema/database names, instance identifiers, and the internal port conventions your local services listen on -- the names your queries are actually written against. Each one says which account and which data estate a repository belongs to, and schema names are directly actionable for anyone who can already reach the estate. Prefer shape-accurate examples with zeroed digits, as here, over live values: the pattern matches any digits, so a real identifier adds nothing to the control and costs you one more identifier in a file you now have to keep back.

classes.name: record or taxonomy noun
classes.counter_example: a recovery plan for the flagship programme
classes.reason: Internal record-ID formats and the taxonomy nouns your domain work is written in. They leak the shape of a portfolio even where no single value is sensitive: a reader can tell how the work is partitioned and how it is numbered. Leave this class CASE-SENSITIVE -- no (?i) -- wherever its lowercase spellings are ordinary English, or it will fire on prose instead of on identifiers. Note that the counter-example here differs from the example's last alternative only in case, which is exactly why the controls use [regex]::IsMatch rather than PowerShell's case-insensitive -match: written the easy way, this control would report the class healthy while the scan walked past every real hit.

classes.name: internal document
classes.reason: Document-host URLs, site-collection paths, and the URI schemes your desktop clients mint for a file held inside the tenant. Each is a working handle on an internal library rather than a mere mention of one, and the odd schemes are the forms an author pastes without registering that they are not ordinary links. The counter-example is an ordinary local file URL, which must keep shipping.
